title: Wi-Fi
desc: Wi-Fi 5/6/6E/7, bands, access points, surveys and security

pages.t: Wi-Fi is built on IEEE 802.11 standards. Instead of cryptic letters, generations now have numbers: Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n), Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac), Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) and Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be).
g: IEEE 802.11
The family of technical standards behind Wi-Fi.
Wi-Fi
A brand and compliance certification for 802.11 wireless networking.

pages.t: Each generation raises the top theoretical speed and handles more devices better. Real speeds are always lower than the headline. The generation matters most when many devices share a place, not when one laptop is on its own.
g: Link rate
The theoretical top speed of a wireless link, not what you will get in daily use.

pages.t: A new access point does not make an old phone faster. Devices and access points both need the generation. Newer gear still works with older devices, they just connect the older way. So selling Wi-Fi 6 or 7 is a common way to future-proof.

quiz.q: Which is the technical name behind Wi-Fi 6?
quiz.w: Wi-Fi 6 is 802.11ax; Wi-Fi 5 is 802.11ac; Wi-Fi 4 is 802.11n.

quiz.q: A customer installs a Wi-Fi 7 access point but all devices are old. What happens?
o: Old devices still connect but with older Wi-Fi
quiz.w: Both ends must support the generation; older devices use older modes.

quiz.q: When does the generation matter most?
o: When many devices share the space
quiz.w: Newer generations handle more simultaneous devices better.

pages.t: The SSID is the Wi-Fi network name that you see in the list. Several access points can share one SSID, so a big office or house looks like one seamless network to users.
g: SSID
Service Set Identifier: the name of a Wi-Fi network.

pages.t: An access point adds Wi-Fi to a wired network. A wireless router combines the router and an access point in one unit. Businesses often prefer separate access points, placed where the coverage is needed.
g: Access point (AP)
Device that connects Wi-Fi devices to the wired network.

pages.t: In a mesh, nodes relay traffic for each other so you can cover an area without a cable to every node. Good for cost-effective coverage and self-healing, but fewer cables to the units means more sharing of radio capacity.
g: Mesh
A network where nodes pass traffic on for one another.
Backhaul
The link carrying traffic from an AP back to the main network.

quiz.q: What is an SSID?
quiz.w: The SSID is the name shown when you search for Wi-Fi.

quiz.q: A wireless router is...
o: A router and access point combined
quiz.w: It combines routing and Wi-Fi access in one device.

quiz.q: What is a mesh network good for?
o: Covering an area without cabling every node
quiz.w: Mesh nodes relay traffic, which saves cabling and can self-heal.

src.l: Wi-Fi NOW: EU releases 480 MHz of 6 GHz

pages.t: 2.4 GHz is the oldest band. Lower frequencies generally travel further, but the band is crowded: Bluetooth gadgets and microwave ovens interfere. It still matters for old and simple devices like smart plugs.
g: GHz
Gigahertz: the radio frequency band Wi-Fi uses.

pages.t: 5 GHz has more channels, so more devices can share the air. Higher frequencies generally have shorter range. It is a main band for modern business Wi-Fi, together with 6 GHz where supported.
g: Channel
A slice of the radio band used by one Wi-Fi network at a time.

pages.t: The 6 GHz band adds a lot of new spectrum: up to 1200 MHz in the US, but Europe has so far opened about 480 MHz. It allows very wide channels and starts out uncrowded. Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 use it, so devices need to support it.

quiz.q: Which band is the most crowded?
quiz.w: 2.4 GHz shares space with Bluetooth, microwaves and many devices.

quiz.q: Which band is only used by Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 devices?
quiz.w: 6 GHz arrived with Wi-Fi 6E and is used by Wi-Fi 7 as well.

quiz.q: Smart plugs in a house with thick walls. Which band do they typically use?
quiz.w: Lower frequency reaches further, so simple devices use 2.4 GHz.

pages.t: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) works in 2.4 and 5 GHz and copes better with many devices. Wi-Fi 6E is the same technology plus the 6 GHz band, giving more room and wide channels.
g: 6E
Wi-Fi 6 extended to the 6 GHz band.

pages.t: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be, 2024) improves all three bands. Highlights: 320 MHz channels in 6 GHz and multi-link operation, which spreads traffic across several links for higher throughput and reliability.
g: Multi-link operation (MLO)
A device using several bands at once.

pages.t: It targets demanding uses like AR/VR, 3D training and ultra-high-definition video, and dense venues. Most small offices run fine on Wi-Fi 6. Fast access points often benefit from multigig ports on the switch.
g: Multigig port
A switch port faster than 1G, such as 2.5G.

quiz.q: What does Wi-Fi 6E add to Wi-Fi 6?
quiz.w: 6E is Wi-Fi 6 plus the 6 GHz band.

quiz.q: What is multi-link operation in Wi-Fi 7?
o: Using several links to raise throughput and reliability
quiz.w: MLO spreads traffic across multiple links.

quiz.q: A 6-person office with laptops and phones asks if Wi-Fi 7 is a must. Best answer?
o: Wi-Fi 6 is usually enough; Wi-Fi 7 is future-proofing
quiz.w: Wi-Fi 7 targets demanding uses; modest sites often do fine with Wi-Fi 6.

pages.t: A standalone access point works on its own and is set up one by one. Fine for a single AP. With many, each unit has its own settings, and it is easy to end up with inconsistent setups.
g: Standalone AP
An AP configured and run on its own, without a controller.

pages.t: A wireless LAN controller manages many APs centrally: settings, security, and smooth hand-over of clients. It can be a central unit, built into APs, or cloud-based. One place to configure replaces touching each AP.
g: Controller
A device or software that manages many access points from one place.

pages.t: Roaming is a device moving from one AP to the next while walking around. APs with the same SSID and security allow it. Good design makes it smooth, so calls and scanners do not drop.
g: Roaming
A device switching between access points without manually reconnecting.

quiz.q: What does a controller do?
quiz.w: A wireless LAN controller centralises AP configuration and management.

quiz.q: A hotel has 60 access points. What do you suggest?
quiz.w: Central management avoids configuring 60 units separately.

quiz.q: What does roaming need?
o: APs sharing the same SSID and security
quiz.w: APs sharing SSID and security let devices move between them.

pages.t: Coverage means signal reaches everywhere. Capacity means enough speed for everyone using it at once. One AP may cover a hall but choke when hundreds connect. Think of room size and of the number of people.
g: Capacity
How many users and how much data the Wi-Fi can serve at once.

pages.t: Walls, floors, metal shelves and water absorb or reflect signal, and an AP often reaches roughly 20 m indoors. Other Wi-Fi, microwaves and cordless phones add interference. So a floor plan alone can mislead.
g: Interference
Other radio signals that disturb your Wi-Fi.

pages.t: A site survey plans AP positions to meet coverage, speed, roaming and call quality. Predictive surveys simulate on a floor plan. On-site surveys measure in the real building. Do it for hotels, warehouses and complaints.
g: Site survey
A planning or audit process measuring Wi-Fi conditions in a real place.

quiz.q: A conference room has full signal but video calls lag when 80 people join. What is the likely issue?
quiz.w: Signal reaches, but there is not enough capacity for that many users.

quiz.q: What does a predictive survey use?
o: Software simulation on a floor plan
Walking with a measuring device only
quiz.w: Predictive surveys model coverage with virtual APs on a plan.

quiz.q: When is a site survey most worth it?
o: Large or tricky sites like hotels and warehouses
quiz.w: Complex sites with many users or obstacles benefit most.

pages.t: WPA2 (2004) is still common. WPA3 (announced 2018) is stronger, with better protection against password guessing, and has been required for Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices since 2020. Choose WPA3 where all devices support it.
g: WPA2/WPA3
Wi-Fi security standards. WPA3 is the newer, stronger one.

pages.t: Personal uses one shared password: good for homes and small offices. Enterprise checks each user via a login server (802.1X, often RADIUS), so you can remove one person without changing everyone's password.
g: RADIUS
A login server that checks who may join the network.

pages.t: A guest network gives visitors internet only, kept apart from staff systems, often with its own SSID and VLAN. For open public Wi-Fi, Enhanced Open encrypts traffic without a shared password.
g: Guest network
A separate Wi-Fi for visitors with no access to internal systems.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of WPA3-Personal?
quiz.w: WPA3-Personal adds protection against password-guessing attacks.

quiz.q: A 200-person company wants to remove a leaver without changing a shared password. What fits?
quiz.w: Enterprise authentication uses individual logins via 802.1X.

quiz.q: What is the main point of a guest network?
o: Visitors get internet but not internal systems
quiz.w: It separates guests from staff systems.

pages.t: One person, few devices. A good wireless router may be enough, or one access point if the router is badly placed. Large houses may need a mesh or wired APs. Wi-Fi 6 is a safe pick today.
Customers, staff, a card terminal and maybe cameras. Use one or two PoE access points, a separate guest SSID, and WPA2/WPA3 for the staff network. Keep payment devices off the guest network.
g: PoE access point
An AP powered through its network cable.

pages.t: How big is the place, and what are the walls like? How many people and devices at peak? What must never fail, like card payments? Is cabling possible? Answers decide AP count and type.

quiz.q: A shop has a card terminal and offers free Wi-Fi. What is wise?
o: Put guests on a separate network from payment devices
quiz.w: Guest traffic should be separate from important internal devices.

quiz.q: A one-person home office in a small flat. What is usually enough?
quiz.w: Small sites with few devices rarely need more than one decent unit.

quiz.q: Which question helps size Wi-Fi?
quiz.w: Peak users and devices drive capacity needs.

pages.t: Many rooms, thick walls, guests streaming at the same time. Plan many APs, wired back to a switch, central management and good roaming. A site survey is strongly advised. Separate guest and staff networks.

Tall metal racks, big open spaces, handheld scanners that must not drop. Metal blocks signal, so APs sit high and carefully placed. Roaming quality and coverage beat top speed. Survey on site, with racks full.
g: Roaming scanner
A handheld that moves between APs while in use.

pages.t: A reseller should offer the survey, the APs with a controller or cloud tool, PoE switches, and outdoor or ruggedised APs where needed. The extras make the project work and protect their reputation.
g: Ruggedised
Built to handle dust, cold or knocks.

quiz.q: Which matters most in a warehouse with handheld scanners?
quiz.w: Scanners move around, so stable coverage and roaming matter more than peak speed.

quiz.q: A hotel has 150 rooms. Which is the best advice?
o: Plan with a site survey and central management
quiz.w: Large sites with many walls need surveyed placement and central control.

quiz.q: Why do metal racks matter?
o: They block signal, so AP placement needs care
quiz.w: Obstacles like metal absorb or reflect radio signals.
